extracted.intended_audience: orators, rhetoricians, poets, historians, and writers seeking to produce sublime/styleful prose or speech
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and evaluative criteria for producing 'the sublime' in prose and oratory—covers diction, figurative language (periphrasis, metaphor), emotional force, ornament, and the trade-off between grandeur and purity of style.

rubrics_metrics.name: Periphrasis contributes to the sublime
rubrics_metrics.description: That periphrasis contributes to the sublime; it often 'chimes in with the literal expression of our meaning and gives it a far richer note'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: like musical ornament enhances the main theme (trills and harmonies bring out the dominant note). Examples cited: Penelope's expanded address, Plato's Funeral Oration, Xenophon. Use periphrasis to add dignity and musicality; do not make it bombastic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of ornament must be proportionate
rubrics_metrics.description: Periphrasis (and other ornaments) is 'a risky business... unless used with a due sense of proportion.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-patterns: overuse causes triviality, flatness, and invites ridicule (critics mock Plato for unseasonable figures). Rule: apply ornament sparingly and with sense of proportion so it enriches without sounding trivial or slow-witted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of the right and fine word (diction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of the right word and the fine word has a marvellously moving and seductive effect upon an audience and is the supreme object of orators and historians.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effects: gives grandeur, beauty, weight, force, strength, and a glittering charm to style ('beautiful words are the very light of thought'). Caution: 'their majesty is not for common use'—do not attach great and stately words to trivial matters (like 'fastening a great tragic mask on a simple child').

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use elevated diction on trivial subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid fastening great and stately words to trivial things—the majesty of lofty diction is inappropriate for ordinary subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern example: calling ordinary possessions 'ovine and bovine treasure' or using tragic grandeur for childish or small matters. Keep high diction reserved for worthy subjects to avoid absurdity and bombast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures of speech lend emotion and excitement
rubrics_metrics.description: All figures (metaphor, periphrasis, etc.) serve to lend emotion and excitement to style; emotion is as much an element in the sublime as character-study is in agreeable writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use figures to increase emotional intensity. They are especially apt in passages that aim at sublimity; their purpose is to move and sweep the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metaphor as a primary vehicle of sublimity
rubrics_metrics.description: Metaphors make for sublimity; 'figurative writing has a natural grandeur and metaphors make for sublimity.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Particularly effective in emotional and descriptive passages. Examples: Herodotus' graphic phrases, Xenophon's anatomy-metaphors, Plato's extensive metaphorical passages. Beware: metaphor tempts excess and bombast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate number/placement of metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Some critics lay down a law that two or at most three metaphors should be used together; however, when 'emotion sweeps on like a flood' more may be acceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guideline: prefer restraint (two–three) in ordinary usage; permit a 'multitude of metaphors' only at moments of genuine, overwhelming emotion or sustained sublimity (Demosthenes is cited as model for many metaphors used in emotional surge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating audacious/bold metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Bold metaphors may be softened by inserting 'as if' or a mild disparagement to mitigate audacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: use qualifiers ('as if', 'as it were') or disclaimers to temper daring figurative expressions so they do not sound intolerably audacious; critics use this to excuse otherwise startling imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Antidote to excessive figurative language: genuine emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper antidote for a multitude of daring metaphors is strong and timely emotion and genuine sublimity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: true emotional force sweeps the audience along and prevents them from examining the number or audacity of metaphors; thus, excess is acceptable only when it coheres with authentic emotional intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustained series of metaphors in description
rubrics_metrics.description: In the treatment of a commonplace and in descriptions there is nothing so expressive as a sustained series of metaphors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Xenophon's anatomical catalogue and Plato's similar descriptive sequences. Use chained metaphors to magnify and animate descriptive passages, but watch for overreach and clarity loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plain or vulgar phrase can be powerfully expressive
rubrics_metrics.description: Vulgar or colloquial phrases, being 'taken from our common life', can be immediately recognized and thus 'halfway to conviction'—they may be more enlightening than elegant language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use familiar, even coarse phrases when vividness and immediate recognition are desired; risk: such phrases 'come perilously near to vulgarity' and must be judged by effect and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Figures and ornament must harmonize with literal meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Ornament should 'chime in with the literal expression of our meaning' and make the expression musical without discordant bombast.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy with musical harmony: ornament should accompany and bring out the dominant thought like trills complement a melody. Avoid ornaments that clash with or obscure the literal sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-off: grandeur with flaws vs. flawless mediocrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Which is better: 'grandeur with a few flaws' or 'correct composition of mediocre quality'? The treatise favors greatness even if not immaculate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Principle: prefer works of 'great excellence' even with occasional slips (attributed to heedlessness of genius) over impeccable but uninspired compositions. Examples: prefer Homer to Apollonius; Pindar/Sophocles to their more faultless rivals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greatness entails risk and occasional oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The greatest natures are least immaculate; 'perfect precision runs the risk of triviality' while greatness necessarily 'lets in casually almost and at random' some oversights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation: mark some tolerance for faults in otherwise sublime writing; penalize only if faults undermine the grandeur. The presence of boldness and lofty effects can outweigh lapses in neatness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use figures in service of emotion, not display
rubrics_metrics.description: Figures (periphrasis, metaphor) are valuable because they add emotion and excitement; they should not be used merely for display or ornamentation that lacks emotional basis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: critics fault Plato for being 'carried away by the intoxication of his language into harsh and intemperate metaphor and allegorical bombast.' Ensure figurative language is motivated by feeling or thought, not gratuitous ornament.
